summary: 4b opens with three tannaitic explanations of what Moses's six-day cloud period at Sinai accomplished: R. Akiva says the cloud covered the mountain (not Moses), and the public calling honored Moses; R. Natan says the cloud purged Moses's food and drink from his system so he could endure 40 days without eating like a ministering angel; R. Matya ben Charash says the cloud intimidated Moses so Torah would be received with awe and trembling, citing a verse that Rav Adda bar Mattana then reads as also teaching that joy and trembling coexist in divine service. The daf then works through the calendar arithmetic: a baraita records a dispute between an anonymous first view (Torah given 6 Sivan) and Rabbi Yosi (7 Sivan); the Gemara reports that R. Yosi HaGalili sides with the anonymous view and R. Akiva with Rabbi Yosi's. R. Akiva's resulting count reaches exactly 40 days ending on 17 Tammuz directly, while R. Yosi HaGalili's reaches the same date only by folding the six days of separation into the 40 rather than adding them beforehand. The sugya then addresses the contradiction between the voice being public at Sinai and private at the Tent of Meeting, resolves how Moses entered the cloud when he could not enter the Tent, and derives two practical rules: call someone's attention before speaking to them, and the word 'lemor' signals that what one is told may not be repeated until the teller gives explicit permission. The page closes with R. Yochanan being identified as the strict opinion on inauguration invalidation, and leaves open the question of practical differences between him and R. Chanina.

display.title: Three readings of the six-day cloud: purification, intimidation, and public honor
display.oneLine: R. Akiva: the cloud covered the mountain, not Moses - the public calling was to honor Moses. R. Natan: the cloud purged Moses's system to render him angelic for 40 days. R. Matya ben Charash: the cloud intimidated Moses so Torah would be received with awe. Rav Adda: joy and trembling are meant to coexist.
display.shortSummary: Three tannaitic readings address why Moses waited six days in the cloud before God called him. R. Akiva says the cloud covered the mountain so the public could witness the call - an honor to Moses. R. Natan focuses on Moses's body: the cloud cleansed food and drink from his system so he could function for 40 days without eating, like a ministering angel. R. Matya ben Charash focuses on Moses's spirit: the cloud created awe and trembling so Torah would be received in fear. Rav Adda bar Mattana adds a Psalm teaching that joy and trembling must coexist in divine encounter.
display.whats: The page opens continuing from 4a's debate over what the six-day cloud period accomplished. R. Akiva (whose view was mentioned on 4a) holds the cloud covered the mountain, not Moses - the purpose was public visibility, so Israel saw the call and it honored Moses. R. Natan disagrees: Moses himself was covered. The purpose was physical - to purge the food and drink from his digestive system so he could ascend the mountain and go 40 days without eating, 'like the ministering angels.' R. Matya ben Charash adds a spiritual reading: the cloud was meant to intimidate Moses, filling him with awe and trembling so he would receive Torah with the proper reverence, and he cites a Psalm verse for this ('serve God with awe and rejoice with trembling'). The Gemara then asks what 'rejoice with trembling' in that same verse means, and Rav Adda bar Mattana, citing Rav, answers: where there is joy, there must also be trembling - the two are not opposites but are meant to coexist in the divine encounter.
display.hint: Three sages read the same six days through three different lenses: honor, physiology, and psychology. Which reading do you find most compelling, and what does each say about what Torah-receiving requires?

learning.learnerQuestion: Why does the Torah record that Moses waited six days before God called him? What was happening during those days?
learning.coreTension: The cloud-period before God's call seems like a delay - but the Gemara insists it served a purpose. Three different purposes are proposed, each reflecting a different view of what Moses needed to be ready.
learning.coreMove: Each tanna identifies a different dimension of preparation: R. Akiva focuses on honor (public witness), R. Natan on physical transformation (like an angel), R. Matya on spiritual preparation (awe). The Gemara presents them side by side without adjudicating between them here. Rashi identifies R. Natan's and R. Matya's readings as following R. Yosi HaGalili's view that there was a real six-day separation before Sinai, and R. Akiva's reading as following his own, opposing view (no separation) - the same dating dispute the next sugya works out explicitly.
learning.resolution: The three readings are presented together rather than one being chosen. Moses needed public recognition (R. Akiva), physical purification (R. Natan), or psychological awe (R. Matya). Per Rashi, R. Natan and R. Matya's readings track R. Yosi HaGalili's chronology while R. Akiva's tracks his own opposing chronology. Rav Adda's addition, answering a follow-up question on R. Matya's own proof-verse, adds that joy and trembling coexist as the emotional tone of divine encounter.

takeaway.text: Preparation for encountering the Divine involves multiple dimensions: public legitimacy, physical readiness, and interior awe. The Psalm adds that joy and trembling are not opposites - they must coexist in genuine religious experience.

reasoningPattern.notes: Three tannaim read the same cloud-period through honor, physiology, and psychology. R. Natan and R. Matya's readings are tied by Rashi to R. Yosi HaGalili's chronology (a real six-day separation), while R. Akiva's reading is tied to his own, opposing chronology (no separation) - so the three views are not freely interchangeable regardless of dating, even though the Gemara presents them side by side without adjudicating here.

learning.ahaMoment: R. Natan's reading is strikingly physical: the cloud didn't just cover Moses, it transformed his body. Six days of cloud-immersion cleansed him so thoroughly he could go 40 days without food - literally becoming angelic. This is preparation at the cellular level, not just spiritual.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may expect one reading to 'win,' or may assume all three are freely combinable regardless of dating. The Gemara presents all three without adjudicating here, but R. Natan's and R. Matya's readings presuppose R. Yosi HaGalili's chronology while R. Akiva's presupposes his own opposing chronology - a tension the next sugya's calendar dispute makes explicit.
learning.memoryAnchor: Three preps, three layers: (1) public call = honor; (2) cloud cleanses food = angel-body; (3) cloud intimidates = awe. Plus: joy and trembling belong together.

argumentFlow.label: R. Akiva: cloud covered the mountain, calling was public honor
argumentFlow.speaker: R. Akiva
argumentFlow.text: The cloud covered the mountain, not Moses. Moses ascended and descended throughout those six days. The public calling on the seventh day was so Israel would see God calling Moses - a public act of honor.

sourceRefs.note: R. Akiva's reading: cloud covers mountain, calling honors Moses

argumentFlow.label: R. Natan: cloud purged Moses's system to render him angelic
argumentFlow.speaker: R. Natan
argumentFlow.text: The cloud covered Moses himself. Its purpose was to purge the food and drink in his system over six days, transforming him so he could go 40 days on the mountain without eating - becoming like the ministering angels.

sourceRefs.note: R. Natan: physical purification to angelic state

argumentFlow.label: R. Matya ben Charash: cloud intimidated Moses for awe-filled Torah reception
argumentFlow.speaker: R. Matya ben Charash
argumentFlow.text: The cloud's purpose was to fill Moses with awe and trembling - so that when he received the Torah he would receive it with fear and reverence, not familiarity.

sourceRefs.note: R. Matya: psychological preparation through intimidation

argumentFlow.label: Rav Adda answers what 'rejoice with trembling' means in R. Matya's own verse
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Adda bar Mattana citing Rav
argumentFlow.text: R. Matya already cited the verse 'serve God with awe and rejoice with trembling' as his proof-text. The Gemara asks what 'rejoice with trembling' itself means, and Rav Adda bar Mattana, citing Rav, answers: where there is joy, there must also be trembling. These are not opposing states - genuine divine encounter combines both.

sourceRefs.note: Rav Adda answers a clarifying question on R. Matya's already-cited verse

conceptRefs.label: Preparation required before entering the Divine Presence

misconceptions.misconception: The three readings about the cloud's purpose are freely combinable regardless of dating.
misconceptions.correction: The Gemara presents all three side by side without choosing between them here, but they are not simply interchangeable: Rashi ties R. Natan's and R. Matya's readings to R. Yosi HaGalili's chronology (a real separation period), while R. Akiva's reading is tied to his own opposing chronology (no separation period) - the same dating dispute the next sugya works out explicitly.

visualizableElements.item: Three-panel diagram of the cloud's purpose: (1) Moses ascending/descending publicly while cloud covers mountain - honor; (2) Cloud surrounding Moses's body with food being cleansed out - angelic transformation; (3) Moses kneeling in awe beneath the cloud - intimidation and trembling
Psalm verse banner: 'Serve God with awe / Rejoice with trembling' - showing the two emotions side by side rather than opposed

quizSeeds.question: What does R. Natan say the six-day cloud accomplished for Moses?
quizSeeds.answer: It physically purged the food and drink from Moses's system over six days, transforming him so he could function for 40 days on the mountain without eating - like a ministering angel who does not need food.

quizSeeds.question: What does Rav Adda bar Mattana add to the discussion of joy and trembling?
quizSeeds.answer: He cites Psalm 2 - 'serve God with awe and rejoice with trembling' - to show that joy and trembling must coexist. Where there is joy in divine service, there must also be trembling. They are not opposites but simultaneous.

alternateAngles: R. Natan's view that the cloud physically transformed Moses into an angelic state raises an interesting question about what it means to receive Torah. If Moses had to become temporarily non-human to receive it, what does that say about the nature of the revelation?

display.title: Calendar arithmetic: 6th vs. 7th Sivan and the 17 Tammuz check
display.oneLine: R. Yosi HaGalili says Torah was given on 6 Sivan; R. Akiva says 7 Sivan. R. Akiva's count reaches exactly 40 days ending on 17 Tammuz directly; R. Yosi HaGalili's reaches the same date only by folding the six sequestering days into the 40 rather than counting them beforehand.
display.shortSummary: A baraita records two views on when Torah was given (an anonymous view: 6 Sivan; Rabbi Yosi: 7 Sivan); the Gemara reports R. Yosi HaGalili sides with the first and R. Akiva with Rabbi Yosi's. This has an arithmetic consequence: R. Akiva's reckoning yields exactly 40 full days ending on 17 Tammuz, the traditional date the tablets were shattered, directly. R. Yosi HaGalili reaches 17 Tammuz too, but only by counting the six preparatory days as part of the 40 rather than in addition to them. The sugya then cites the verse's phrasing, together with Israel's presence, in 'vayikra el Moshe, Moshe... ve-chol Yisrael omdin' as support for R. Elazar's reading that the public call was meant to honor Moses.
display.whats: The Gemara asks which position - R. Yosi HaGalili's 6th Sivan or R. Akiva's 7th Sivan - is consistent with the tradition that Moses shattered the tablets on 17 Tammuz. A baraita first states two unattributed views: an anonymous first view holds Torah was given on the 6th of Sivan; Rabbi Yosi (a different sage from Rabbi Yosi HaGalili) holds the 7th. The Gemara then reports that R. Yosi HaGalili sides with the anonymous view and R. Akiva sides with Rabbi Yosi's. R. Akiva's resulting count: Torah given on 7 Sivan. Six days of Sivan had already passed, and Moses ascended on the 7th. Remaining days in Sivan: 24 (days 7-30, counting the 7th itself as the first of the forty). Plus 16 days in Tammuz (1-16) = 40 days. He descends into the 17th = 17 Tammuz. This works perfectly. R. Yosi HaGalili's count: Torah given on 6 Sivan, then Moses sequestered for 6 more days, ascending later in Sivan. Counted straightforwardly, his sequence would not reach the tablets' breaking until 23 Tammuz - past the 40-day mark relative to 17 Tammuz. R. Yosi HaGalili resolves this by folding the six sequestering days into the 40 (rather than adding them beforehand), which brings his count to 17 Tammuz as well. The sugya then cites the verse's phrasing and 'all Israel were standing' as support for R. Elazar's reading that the public call was meant to honor Moses - not that all Israel heard the voice itself.
display.hint: The calendar arithmetic is not just a puzzle - it functions as evidence. Which opinion does the 17 Tammuz tradition support, and how does the Gemara handle the loser's arithmetic?

learning.learnerQuestion: Why does the Gemara use the 17 Tammuz tablet-shattering date as a test for the Sinai calendar dispute?
learning.coreTension: R. Yosi HaGalili and R. Akiva disagree by one day on when Torah was given. The dispute seems trivial - until you realize the 40-day count on the mountain must end on 17 Tammuz. That external fixed point turns the calendar dispute into a testable claim.
learning.coreMove: Use the 17 Tammuz tradition (when the tablets were shattered - a fixed and well-known date) as a calendar check. Count backward 40 days. Whichever opinion produces 40 days ending exactly on 17 Tammuz wins the arithmetic argument.
learning.resolution: R. Akiva's count works: 7 Sivan + 24 days remaining in Sivan + 16 days of Tammuz = exactly 40 days, arriving at 17 Tammuz. R. Yosi HaGalili's count only works if the 6 preparation days are included within the 40.

takeaway.text: A tannaitic dispute can be tested against a fixed historical date. If only one opinion is arithmetically consistent with a known tradition (17 Tammuz), that is evidence - though not proof - in its favor. The losing opinion must then account for the discrepancy.

reasoningPattern.notes: Use a fixed external date as a constraint on an otherwise underdetermined dispute. The arithmetic eliminates one reading or forces it into an awkward accounting.

learning.ahaMoment: The 40-day count is not just a nice round number - it is a constraint that the calendar must satisfy. R. Akiva's 7 Sivan starting point produces 24 + 16 = 40 exactly. R. Yosi HaGalili's 6 Sivan starting point overshoots or undershoots unless he folds the preparation days into the count.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may not see why the 17 Tammuz date matters. It functions like carbon dating: an external fixed point against which competing chronologies are tested.
learning.memoryAnchor: R. Akiva's math: 7 Sivan up + 24 days left in Sivan + 16 in Tammuz = 40 on the dot, landing on 17 Tammuz when the tablets broke. R. Yosi HaGalili's math only works if he borrows from the preparation days.

argumentFlow.label: What do R. Yosi HaGalili and R. Akiva disagree about?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara asks what R. Yosi HaGalili and R. Akiva actually disagree about: a baraita states two views - an anonymous first view holds Torah was given on the 6th of Sivan; Rabbi Yosi (a different sage from Rabbi Yosi HaGalili) holds the 7th. The Gemara then reports that Rabbi Yosi HaGalili sides with the anonymous view (6th) and Rabbi Akiva sides with Rabbi Yosi's view (7th). The sugya will test this one-day difference against the fixed tradition that the tablets were shattered on 17 Tammuz, 40 days later.

sourceRefs.note: Introduces the 6th-vs-7th-Sivan dispute that the 17 Tammuz check will test

argumentFlow.label: R. Akiva's count works: 24 + 16 = 40
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: According to R. Akiva: Torah given on 7 Sivan; six days of Sivan had already passed, and Moses ascended on the 7th. 24 days remain in Sivan (days 7-30, counting the 7th itself as the first of the forty). 16 days of Tammuz (1-16). Total: 40 full days. He descends on 17 Tammuz. This matches the tradition perfectly.

sourceRefs.note: R. Akiva's arithmetic: 24 + 16 = 40, ending 17 Tammuz

argumentFlow.label: R. Yosi HaGalili's count doesn't reach 17 Tammuz
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: According to R. Yosi HaGalili: Torah was given on 6 Sivan. Moses sequestered 6 more days, ascending on 13 Sivan. Counted straightforwardly, this reaches only 23 Tammuz for the 40th day - not 17 Tammuz - unless the 6 preparation days are folded into the count.

sourceRefs.note: R. Yosi HaGalili's arithmetic problem

argumentFlow.label: R. Yosi HaGalili includes the preparation days within the 40
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: R. Yosi HaGalili's count only works if the 6 sequestering days are included within the 40 days Moses spent on the mountain - they are not prior to the 40 but part of them.

sourceRefs.note: R. Yosi HaGalili's resolution: sequestering days are inside the 40

argumentFlow.label: Public calling honored Moses - R. Elazar's view confirmed
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The master recalls: 'Vayikra el Moshe, Moshe, ve-chol Yisrael omdin' - the verse's phrasing, together with Israel's presence nearby. This supports R. Elazar's reading: the context of a public calling before Israel shows the verse's purpose was only to give Moses public honor, not that Israel heard the content of what was said.

sourceRefs.note: Public call as honor to Moses

conceptRefs.label: Calendar arithmetic as a test of tannaitic positions

misconceptions.misconception: The 6th vs. 7th Sivan dispute is a minor detail with no consequences.
misconceptions.correction: The one-day difference determines whether a 40-day count lands on 17 Tammuz (when tablets were shattered) directly or only by folding the six preparation days into the count. R. Akiva's 7 Sivan count reaches 17 Tammuz directly; R. Yosi HaGalili's 6 Sivan count only reaches it once those days are counted as part of the 40. The dispute has a testable arithmetic consequence either way.

visualizableElements.item: Calendar timeline: Sivan 1-30 and Tammuz 1-17, with R. Akiva's count marked (day 7 start, 24 remaining, +16 = 40, hits 17 Tammuz) vs. R. Yosi HaGalili's count (day 6 start, different endpoint)
Shattered tablets icon on 17 Tammuz as the fixed anchor point from which the arithmetic works backward

quizSeeds.question: How does R. Akiva's calendar work out to 40 complete days ending on 17 Tammuz?
quizSeeds.answer: Torah was given on 7 Sivan; six days of Sivan had already passed, and Moses ascended the same day. 24 days remained in Sivan (days 7-30, counting the 7th itself as the first of the forty). Plus 16 days in Tammuz (1-16) = 40 full days. Moses descended on 17 Tammuz - the day the tablets were shattered.

quizSeeds.question: How does R. Yosi HaGalili reconcile his position with the 17 Tammuz tradition?
quizSeeds.answer: He must include the 6 sequestering days within the 40-day count. The preparation days are not prior to the 40 - they are part of it. Only by counting from the beginning of the preparation period does his arithmetic reach 17 Tammuz.

display.title: Public vs. private voice; Moses enters the cloud; calling before speaking; 'lemor' as confidentiality
display.oneLine: Two independent answers resolve Sinai's public voice vs. the Tent's private voice: either the difference is Sinai vs. the Tent (location), or between the call and the speech itself (content) - not a single combined answer. Moses entered the cloud either because God pulled him in (R. Elazar) or, per a gezerah shavah from the sea-parting, by walking through an opening. The verse 'vayikra vayedaber' teaches: always announce yourself before speaking. The word 'lemor' teaches that what you are told may not be repeated until you are given permission.
display.shortSummary: A contradiction between Sinai (public voice) and the Tent of Meeting (private voice only Moses heard) is resolved two independent ways: either the difference is Sinai vs. the Tent, or the difference is between the call and the speech itself. How did Moses enter the Tent when blocked by the cloud? Two independent answers: R. Elazar says God grabbed him in; the school of R. Yishmael derives via a gezerah shavah from the sea-parting that 'betoch' means passage through, not immersion. Two practical rules follow from the opening verse: 'vayikra el Moshe vayedaber' teaches you should always call before speaking; the word 'lemor' teaches that what is told to you may not be repeated until the teller gives permission.
display.whats: The Gemara faces a textual contradiction: at Sinai the call was public, but at the Tent of Meeting the verse says the voice was heard 'by him alone' (kol lo, Moses heard but Israel did not). The Gemara gives two independent resolutions, either of which removes the contradiction: (1) the difference is between the two settings - at Sinai it was public, at the Tent it was private; or (2) if you prefer, the difference is between the call and the speech - the calling itself, not just the content, is what differs. A second problem: Moses could not enter the Tent of Meeting (blocked by the cloud per Exodus 40), yet the opening verse of Leviticus has God speaking to Moses from the Tent. How did Moses get in? Two independent answers: R. Elazar (via R. Zerika) says God reached out and pulled Moses into the cloud. The school of R. Yishmael instead derives from a gezerah shavah with the sea crossing - 'betoch' means a path through (as Israel walked betoch the sea, through a dry channel), not literal immersion - that Moses likewise walked through an opening in the cloud. The verse 'vayikra el Moshe vayedaber Hashem' teaches derekh eretz: one should always call someone to attention before speaking to them. Finally, the word 'lemor' at the end of this communication is read to mean that a person who tells you something puts you under a prohibition to repeat it until they explicitly tell you 'go and say it.'
display.hint: The Gemara resolves the same contradiction two independent ways rather than picking one - what does that tell you about how the sugya treats 'lo kashya, ha... ha...' answers? And the 'lemor' derivation yields a real behavioral norm from what looks like a technical closing word - what does that say about the relationship between a verse's plain sense and its legal derivation?

learning.learnerQuestion: How can the same voice be both public (at Sinai) and private (at the Tent)? Weren't both cases God speaking to Moses?
learning.coreTension: The Torah says the voice at the Tent was heard only by Moses - but at Sinai the call was public. Both involve God speaking to Moses. How can the same divine communication function differently?
learning.coreMove: The Gemara offers two independent, alternative resolutions rather than one combined answer: either the difference is the setting (Sinai vs. the Tent), or the difference is which part of the communication is meant (the call vs. the speech). Either alone removes the contradiction.
learning.resolution: Two independent answers are given. First: Sinai required public witness to honor Moses, while the ongoing Tent of Meeting communications were private by design - a setting-based distinction. Second (an alternative, not an addition): the calling itself differed in publicity from the speaking that followed - a content-based distinction. The Gemara does not combine these into one claim.

takeaway.text: Two practical norms are derived from the Leviticus verse: (1) always call someone's attention before speaking to them (derekh eretz, from 'vayikra vayedaber'); (2) a person who tells you something puts you under a prohibition to repeat it until they explicitly permit it (from the word 'lemor').

reasoningPattern.notes: The sugya resolves a contradiction with two independent 'lo kashya' answers (setting-based and content-based), then separately derives two independent behavioral norms from close reading of the same verse.

learning.ahaMoment: The 'lemor' derivation flips the word's apparent function: rather than a plain instruction to transmit the message, the Gemara reads it as establishing that transmission requires explicit permission first. This transforms a routine closing word into a principle of information ethics - you are the temporary custodian of what you hear, not its owner.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may read 'lemor' as simply 'say it' (its plain sense) and miss that the Gemara derives a permission-based restriction from it, or may assume the Gemara's two answers to the public/private contradiction combine into one claim when they are independent alternatives.
learning.memoryAnchor: Vayikra then vayedaber: call first, speak second. Always announce yourself. And 'lemor': what you heard belongs to the teller until they say 'go and say it.'

argumentFlow.label: Contradiction: public at Sinai, private at the Tent
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: 'Vayikra el Moshe vayedaber' - all Israel heard the call at Sinai. But at the Tent the verse says 'kol lo' - the voice went to him alone, not heard by Israel. How can the same divine voice be public in one place and private in another?

sourceRefs.note: Contradiction between public Sinai call and private Tent voice

argumentFlow.label: Two independent resolutions: setting-based, or call-vs-speech-based
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara gives two independent answers, either of which removes the contradiction on its own. First: this (private) is at the Tent, this (public) is at Sinai - a setting-based distinction. Alternatively (the Gemara's own 've-i ba'it eima'): this is about the calling (kria), this is about the speaking (dibbur) - at Sinai the call itself was public even though speech content could still be private. These are two separate ways to resolve the difficulty, not two parts of one combined claim.

sourceRefs.note: Two independent 'lo kashya' resolutions: location-based and call/speech-based

argumentFlow.label: How did Moses enter the Tent when the cloud blocked him?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Exodus 40 says Moses could not enter the Tent because the cloud rested on it. Yet Leviticus opens with God speaking to Moses from the Tent. How did Moses get in?

sourceRefs.note: Contradiction: Moses blocked from Tent yet speaks with God there

argumentFlow.label: Two independent answers: R. Elazar's forcible entry vs. the school of R. Yishmael's gezerah shavah
argumentFlow.speaker: R. Elazar / School of R. Yishmael
argumentFlow.text: Two independent answers are given. R. Elazar (via R. Zerika): God reached out and pulled Moses into the cloud and into the Tent. Separately, the school of R. Yishmael derives via a gezerah shavah: just as Israel walked 'betoch' the sea through a dry path (not submerged in water), 'betoch' the cloud means Moses walked through an opening in it, not immersed within it.

sourceRefs.note: Two answers to Moses entering the cloud

argumentFlow.label: Call before speaking: derekh eretz from 'vayikra vayedaber'
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The verse says 'vayikra el Moshe' (He called to Moses) and then 'vayedaber' (He spoke). Why mention calling before speaking? To teach that one should always call someone's attention - address them by name or signal - before speaking to them. This is proper etiquette (derekh eretz).

sourceRefs.note: Calling before speaking as a behavioral norm

argumentFlow.label: 'Lemor' teaches: a hearer may not repeat what he was told until given explicit permission
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rabba (the source's bracketed text gives an alternate, textually uncertain attribution) asks: from where do we know that someone who tells another something puts him under a prohibition to repeat it, until he is told 'go and say it'? From the verse: 'And God spoke to him from the Tent of Meeting, lemor' - the word 'lemor' here is read to establish that permission to transmit is required, not assumed.

sourceRefs.note: 'Lemor' as 'lo emor' - confidentiality norm

conceptRefs.label: Proper social conduct derived from Torah behavior
Lemor as lo emor - information is confidential until permission is granted

misconceptions.misconception: 'Lemor' simply means 'say it' - a command to transmit the message to Israel.
misconceptions.correction: The Gemara derives from the word 'lemor' in this verse that a person who is told something is under a prohibition to repeat it until he is explicitly told 'go and say it.' What you hear from another is theirs to share, not yours, until they give permission.

visualizableElements.item: Two-path diagram: the same public/private contradiction resolved two independent ways - path A (Sinai vs. Tent, setting-based) and path B (calling vs. speaking, content-based) - shown as alternatives, not combined

Word study: the closing word 'lemor' with an arrow to the derived rule 'do not repeat what you were told until given explicit permission' - showing how the derivation works from the word's role in the verse

quizSeeds.question: How does the Gemara resolve the contradiction between the voice being public at Sinai and private at the Tent of Meeting?
quizSeeds.answer: It gives two independent answers. First: the difference is the setting - at Sinai it was public, at the Tent it was private. Alternatively: the difference is between the kria (call) and the dibbur (speech) - the calling itself, not just the content, is what differed. These are two separate resolutions, not one combined claim.

quizSeeds.question: What behavioral principle is derived from 'lemor' in God's communications with Moses?
quizSeeds.answer: From the word 'lemor,' the Gemara derives that a person who tells you something puts you under a prohibition to repeat it until they explicitly tell you 'go and say it.' Information someone shares with you is not yours to transmit until they give permission.

alternateAngles: The two practical norms derived here (call before speaking; lemor = confidentiality) are unusual in that they are derived from divine communication patterns and applied to ordinary human interaction. This treats God's speech acts as models for human etiquette - Torah as a manual for interpersonal behavior, not just law.

display.title: R. Yochanan identified as the strict position on inauguration invalidation
display.oneLine: An earlier exchange between Reish Lakish and R. Yochanan (unrefuted, so treated as conceded) established that inauguration requirements can invalidate. The Gemara then cites a separately-transmitted R. Yochanan/R. Chanina dispute over the scope of that rule, and uses the earlier exchange to identify R. Yochanan as the strict opinion - so, by elimination, R. Chanina holds the narrower one. The page closes with an open question about their practical differences.
display.shortSummary: The Gemara recalls that an earlier exchange - Reish Lakish's challenge to R. Yochanan, which R. Yochanan did not refute - already established that inauguration requirements can invalidate the service. Separately, a dispute is cited between R. Yochanan and R. Chanina: one holds all written inauguration requirements invalidate; the other holds only requirements that also invalidate ongoing service invalidate. Because R. Yochanan's earlier silence matches the strict view, the Gemara concludes he holds it - and, by elimination, R. Chanina holds the narrower one. The sugya closes by asking what their practical disagreements actually are - a question left open, continuing into 5a.
display.whats: The Gemara opens by recalling that 'it follows that both of them' - Reish Lakish and R. Yochanan, from an earlier exchange - hold that the inauguration passage's written requirements can invalidate the service; this follows because Reish Lakish's challenge assumed it and R. Yochanan did not object. Separately, the Gemara cites a transmitted dispute: R. Yochanan and R. Chanina disagreed about this same question - one held that everything written concerning the inauguration invalidates; the other held that only something that also invalidates ongoing service in later generations invalidates the inauguration. The two positions are not yet attributed by name. The Gemara then concludes: it must be R. Yochanan who holds the strict view, since that is exactly the position Reish Lakish assumed he held earlier, and R. Yochanan did not respond to challenge it at all. By elimination, R. Chanina holds the narrower position. The page ends with the question: in concrete cases, what exactly do they disagree about? - left open, continuing to 5a.

learning.learnerQuestion: How do we know which of R. Yochanan and R. Chanina is the strict opinion, when the dispute itself doesn't say which sage held which side?
learning.coreTension: A transmitted dispute states two positions on inauguration invalidation without saying which sage holds which. The Gemara must infer who holds which view from an earlier, separate exchange and from a silence in it.
learning.coreMove: An earlier exchange already established (via Reish Lakish's unrefuted challenge to R. Yochanan) that the strict view - all written inauguration requirements invalidate - is out there and unrefuted. When the Gemara cites the actual R. Yochanan/R. Chanina dispute, it matches that earlier, already-established strict view to R. Yochanan, and assigns R. Chanina the remaining, narrower position by elimination.
learning.resolution: R. Yochanan is identified as the strict position: all written inauguration requirements invalidate. R. Chanina, by elimination, holds the narrower position: only requirements shared with ongoing service invalidate. The identification rests on matching an earlier unrefuted assumption to one side of a separately-cited dispute.

takeaway.text: In Talmudic debate, silence in the face of an accusation or characterization is treated as concession. When R. Yochanan did not refute Reish Lakish's assumption about his position, the Gemara takes that as confirmation of the strict reading.

reasoningPattern.notes: The Gemara reads R. Yochanan's earlier non-refutation of Reish Lakish's challenge as an implicit acceptance of that characterization, then uses that already-settled fact to resolve which side of a separately-cited dispute he is on. This is a standard Talmudic inference pattern.

learning.ahaMoment: The Gemara is doing detective work: a transmitted dispute doesn't say who holds which view. It solves this not from anything in the dispute itself, but by reaching back to an earlier, separate exchange where R. Yochanan's silence in the face of an accusation already revealed his position.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may assume 'both of them' at the start refers to R. Yochanan and R. Chanina - it actually refers back to Reish Lakish and R. Yochanan from an earlier exchange. Keeping that recap separate from the actual R. Yochanan/R. Chanina dispute is essential to following the identification.

glossary.en: Ministering angels. R. Natan's reading: the six-day cloud period physically transformed Moses so he would not need food or drink during his forty days on the mountain - literally angelic status.

The stone tablets. The Gemara uses the 17 Tammuz tradition (when Moses shattered the tablets) as a calendar check on the Sinai debate - which opinion gives the mathematically consistent account of the 40 days on the mountain?

Literally 'to say.' From this closing word in 'and God spoke to him from the Tent of Meeting, lemor,' the Gemara derives a principle of information confidentiality: a person who tells you something puts you under a prohibition to repeat it until they explicitly tell you 'go and say it.'

Invalidation. If a requirement 'me'akkev,' omitting it invalidates the entire service. The dispute between R. Yochanan and R. Chanina about the inauguration is precisely which requirements rise to this level of indispensability.

rashiTranslations.en: 'And the cloud covered it' - the mountain, and not Moses, for during all those six days he went up and came down
early in the morning to say to them 'You have seen what I did to Egypt' (Exodus 19),
'and Moses brought back the words of the people to the Lord'; and the next day it was said to him 'Go to the people
and sanctify them'; and the next day 'Go down, warn the people'. 'And the verse comes only' - to say 'and He called
to Moses' alone, but rather to accord him honor.
'To purge the food and drink' - Rabbi Natan holds
like Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, that the separation was for Moses,
but one is not to learn from here that the others
who enter the camp of the Divine Presence require separation, for
this separation was only that during these six
days the food in his innards was purged,
so as to be like the ministering angels; but in general
we do not require purging. 'To put fear upon him' -
he too holds like Rabbi Yosei HaGelili,
that the separation was for Moses, and to set him apart from
people, so that awe should fall upon him when he is
alone; he will understand and set his heart to enter the camp
of the Divine Presence in awe. 'In the place of joy' - the giving
of the Torah of the tablets, as it is written (Psalms 19):
'the precepts of the Lord are upright, gladdening the heart'. 'In what'
'do they disagree' - what proof do they bring
for their words. 'The Torah was given' - the Ten
Commandments; and from verses they derive their reasons, the first
tanna and Rabbi Yosei, in tractate Shabbat, chapter
Rabbi Akiva. 'The one who says on the sixth' etc. - it is
taught here incidentally, and it was an explanation in the books, so
that it should not trouble you below: how were completed
the forty days on the seventeenth of Tammuz, when the tablets were broken.
'On the seventh he ascended' - to receive the tablets, and he remained
forty days. 'Rabbi Yosei HaGelili holds'
'like the first tanna' - therefore, perforce, the six
days and the seventh day were perforce
after the Ten Commandments; and Moses separated
six days, and on the seventh he entered to receive
the tablets. 'And Rabbi Akiva holds like Rabbi Yosei' -
therefore this seventh was the seventh of the month.
'Granted, according to Rabbi Akiva' - who says there was no separation
there; it is forty days and no more, and they were completed
on the seventeenth of Tammuz: twenty-four of Sivan, for six
days of it had passed and on the seventh he ascended; and however much
of the seventh he entered when he ascended, he was delayed
from descending until within the seventeenth of Tammuz, which is forty
complete. "'A voice to him', 'a voice unto him'" - 'and he heard
the voice speaking unto him' (Numbers 7);
he could have said 'to him', yet it wrote 'speaking unto him',
to teach you that to him alone the voice was drawn.
'In the Tent of Meeting' - once the Tabernacle was erected and He spoke
with him from above the ark cover, the voice was not
heard by Israel; for this verse of 'and he heard
the voice' is written about the Tent of Meeting: the beginning
of the verse is 'and when Moses came into the Tent of Meeting'
etc. 'That he is under a prohibition to tell' etc. - the verse
states 'saying' - do not repeat the words
unless he gives him permission.
'It follows that both of them' etc. - it refers back above,
from what Reish Lakish said to Rabbi Yochanan:
'if so, just as with the inauguration, all that is written concerning them'
etc., and he conceded to him; it follows that both of them, etc.
'And let it be concluded' - the dispute of Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi
Chanina, who disagree about this matter in general: let it be concluded from here that Rabbi Yochanan is the one who says that all that is written concerning them is indispensable.
'Something' - the daf ends mid-word here; Rashi's comment continues on 5a, where the lemma is completed as 'Something that does not invalidate for future generations.'
